title: Flat Base Breakout
teaches: The flat base breakout as we trade it: a leader rests in a box near its highs above the 50-day and 200-day, the pivot is the base's highest high, the buy is the trade through it at market in regular hours, the stop sits a few cents under the breakout day's low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail, and a loss taken at the stop is the system working.

facts.quote: One, two or three weeks do not get the job done.
facts.claim: IBD: one, two or three weeks do not make a base.

facts.quote: The stock's price declines no more than 15% from its intraday peak to intraday trough.
facts.claim: IBD: a flat base declines no more than 15% from its intraday peak to its intraday trough.

facts.quote: The correction within a flat base should be no more than 15% from its intraday high to the bottom of the pattern.
facts.claim: IBD: the correction inside a flat base is no more than 15%.

facts.quote: It should look like a rectangular box with a correction from high to low of no more than 15%.
facts.claim: IBD: a flat base looks like a rectangular box.

facts.quote: the "flat" base has kind of a "U" shape and doesn't look so flat.
facts.claim: IBD allows a flat base with a slight U shape.

facts.quote: Flat bases should show tight trading.
facts.claim: IBD: flat bases should show tight trading.

facts.quote: These shallow patterns often start forming as a stock takes a breather after an earlier advance.
facts.claim: IBD: a flat base forms as a stock rests after an earlier advance.

facts.quote: In a weekly chart, look for periods of sideways movement or mild declines following a prior uptrend of at least 30% in price.
facts.claim: IBD: look for sideways movement after a prior uptrend of at least 30% (stated for any base).

facts.quote: The typical buy point is the price high made before the decline, plus 10 cents.
facts.claim: IBD's buy point is the high before the decline plus 10 cents.

facts.quote: To get the proper buy point, add 10 cents to the highest price in the pattern, which is usually the start of the base.
facts.claim: IBD's buy point is 10 cents above the highest price in the pattern, usually the start of the base.

facts.quote: The buy point in a flat base is 10 cents above the left-side high.
facts.claim: IBD: the flat base buy point is 10 cents above the left-side high.

facts.quote: Sometimes you can draw a trend line connecting at least three points along the top of the base and find the lowest potential entry.
facts.claim: IBD draws a line across at least three points along the top of the base.

facts.quote: you want to see volume bulge at least 40%-50% above average when a stock breaks out of the flat base.
facts.claim: IBD wants breakout volume at least 40% to 50% above average.

facts.quote: A breakout needs to produce a gain of at least 20% in order to be counted as one stage.
facts.claim: IBD: a breakout counts as a stage only if it gained at least 20%.

facts.quote: Breakouts from late-stage bases will often blow up.
facts.claim: IBD: breakouts from late-stage bases often blow up.

facts.quote: It's usually best to buy when a stock breaks out from a first-stage or second-stage base.
facts.claim: IBD: it is usually best to buy a first-stage or second-stage base.

facts.quote: One guideline is the 7%-8% sell rule.
facts.claim: IBD's general loss limit is the 7% to 8% sell rule.

facts.quote: Flat bases form over a 5 to 65 week range. The minimum depth is 0% with a maximum of 15%.
facts.claim: MarketSmith: a flat base is 5 to 65 weeks long and 0% to 15% deep.

facts.quote: Flat bases often occur after a stock runs up after breaking out of one of the other chart patterns.
facts.claim: MarketSmith: flat bases often follow a run-up out of another pattern.

facts.quote: In the case of a Cup, Flat Base, Consolidation or IPO Base, the Pivot corresponds to the Left Side High that began the base.
facts.claim: MarketSmith: a flat base's pivot is the left-side high that began the base.

facts.quote: In most cases, it is the highest intra-day price over the last 100 days (or 20 weeks)
facts.claim: MarketSmith: the left-side high is usually the highest intraday price of the last 100 days.

facts.quote: The percent decline from the start of the base (left side high) to the bottom (intraday low) of the base.
facts.claim: MarketSmith measures depth from the left-side high to the base's intraday low.

facts.quote: Stocks emerging from third, fourth or later stage bases are late in their moves and may be more likely to fail.
facts.claim: MarketSmith: third, fourth or later stage bases are late and more likely to fail.

facts.quote: The Base Stage and Count are always reset to 1 once an intraday low price undercuts the low of the previous base.
facts.claim: MarketSmith: the base count resets to 1 when price undercuts the prior base's low.

facts.quote: The Pivot Range is 0% to 5% above the pivot point
facts.claim: MarketSmith's buy range is 0% to 5% above the pivot.

facts.quote: A prior uptrend of 30% or more: This is the initial strong move that leads into the consolidation phase.
facts.claim: TraderLion: a prior uptrend of 30% or more leads into the base.

facts.quote: the stock's price should not fall more than 15% from its highest point within the base.

facts.quote: the trading volume should be at least 40% higher than its average volume (1.4 times the relative volume).

facts.claim: TraderLion: a well-formed flat base is tight and orderly.

facts.claim: TraderLion: flat base breakouts do better in a strong, bullish market.

facts.claim: Kullamagi: the stop is the low of the day and no wider than the stock's ATR or ADR.

facts.claim: A13: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

facts.claim: Our stop may move up to breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.

walkthroughs.title: NUS, September 2013: the textbook shelf
steps: NUS nearly doubled, then rested six weeks in a tight shelf, only 10.3% deep. It tapped 90 three times.
Friday's candle is a hammer and an inside day, right under 90. That's a good look and a possible buy day.
September 9, 2013, it trades through 90 on 1.9 times normal volume. Buy at market, 90.01. Stop under the day's low, 88.22.
A tad extended from the 50-day, but the stop's only 2.0% away. It hit 3R the next session, and you hold it.

walkthroughs.title: ALLY, June 2019: tight at the end
steps: ALLY in June 2019. After a 31% run it rested 11.2 weeks, only 5.5% deep, the shallowest base we studied.
Four taps of 30, then inside days right into the breakout. That's what tight at the end looks like.
June 27 it clears 30 on 1.8 times volume. Buy at market, 30.28. Stop just under the prior day's low, 29.79.
A close back in the base is the warning sign. It ground to 3R by day 10 instead. Slow still pays.

walkthroughs.title: WSM, September 2023: the throwback after the push
steps: WSM ran 30%, then built an 8-week shelf, 14.6% deep, with four taps of the top.
September 25, 2023, it breaks out on 4.99 times volume. We buy at market, 73.16, stop under the day's low, 72.24.
It runs past 3R that same day. Day 1 is too soon to sell. By day 10, up 5R, you sell some.
Late October it throws back to 71.56, under the original stop. Lots of breakouts do. Then it runs to 99.

questions.q: What are you looking at here?
choices: A leader resting near its highs
A V-shaped bottom after a crash
A pole that doubled in a few weeks
A stock drifting under its 200-day
questions.answer: A leader resting near its highs
questions.why: A leader resting near its highs. That's a flat base. Look left and you see a strong run. Then it goes sideways just under its high, over a rising 50-day and 200-day. Nobody's dumping it. That's what I want, because the rest gives you two things. A clear high to buy through, and a stop that sits close, a few cents under the breakout day's low. A V-bottom or a stock under its 200-day gives you neither.
questions.lesson_line: A flat base is a leader resting near its highs. The high is your trigger, the buy day's low your stop.

wrong.A V-shaped bottom after a crash: That's a stock coming off a low. This one is up near its highs after a run.
wrong.A pole that doubled in a few weeks: That's the run into a flag. Here the run is done and the stock has been resting for weeks.
wrong.A stock drifting under its 200-day: Price is above its 200-day here. Under it, we don't buy stocks at all.

questions.simple: It's a leader resting near its highs, so you get a clear high to buy through and a close stop.
questions.story: The day before the breakout. Check the right side of the chart, then what came before it.

deeper.counter: IBD describes a flat base as a rectangular box that forms as a stock takes a breather after an earlier advance. Bonde calls it a Darvas box. Same picture, different names.

questions.q: Where's the pivot on this base?
choices: Right around $59, the top
Around $55, the bottom
Around $57, mid-range
Around $56, at the 50-day
questions.answer: Right around $59, the top
questions.why: Right around $59. That's the price it kept running into and getting turned back, so that's where the sellers sit. Now look at the last candle. It's a hammer: it dipped, buyers stepped in, and it closed near its high, just under $59. That's a very good look and a possible buy day. When price trades through $59, you buy at market. Your stop goes a few cents under that day's low. Set the alert at $59 tonight, so you buy the break and don't chase it.
questions.lesson_line: The pivot is the high it keeps failing at. Say it in dollars and set the alert there.

wrong.Around $55, the bottom: That's the floor of the range. It tells you where the base breaks down, not where you buy.
wrong.Around $57, mid-range: Halfway up is still inside the range. Nothing has broken out there.
wrong.Around $56, at the 50-day: The 50-day is the trend under the base. It's not the trigger.

questions.simple: The pivot is right around $59, the high it keeps failing at. The hammer just under it looks good.

deeper.counter: MarketSmith calls the pivot the left-side high that began the base. IBD adds 10 cents to it. With a market order the 10 cents doesn't matter. We mark the high itself and buy as price trades through it.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.story: The day before the breakout. You're marking your levels for tomorrow.

questions.q: On a flat base breakout the stop goes a few cents under the base low.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The stop goes a few cents under the breakout day's low. The base low is not the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the breakout day's low.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: On our card the breakout day has price above the 50-day and the ___-day, and the 50-day sits above that line.
questions.why: 200. On the breakout day price is above the 50-day and the 200-day, and the 50-day is above the 200-day. The rulebook also bars longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long. The 50-over-200 order is our own setup test.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 50, above the 200, and the 50 over the 200. Then look at the box.
questions.simple: The blank is 200, because price must sit above the 50-day and the 200-day with the 50 above the 200.

questions.q: This morning it trades through $21.75. How do you take it?
choices: Market order, stop under today's low
Wait for the close, stop under the range
Market order, stop under the range low
Wait for a pullback to the 50-day
questions.answer: Market order, stop under today's low
questions.why: Market order as it goes through $21.75, stop a few cents under today's low. That's the spot you trade against on a buy day: the high you buy through and the low you stop under. Here the stop goes at 21.18, about 2.6% away. It's a tad extended from the 50-day, but with a stop that close I'll take it. Wait for the close and you pay more with the same stop, so you buy fewer shares. A stop under the bottom of the range is way too wide. This was CMG. It made 3R by day 11.
questions.lesson_line: Trade against a spot on a buy day: the high you buy through, the low you stop under.

wrong.Wait for the close, stop under the range: You pay more at the close, and a stop under the bottom of the range is far too wide. Buy it as it goes through.
wrong.Market order, stop under the range low: Right buy, wrong stop. The bottom of the range is way too far away. Your stop goes under today's low.
wrong.Wait for a pullback to the 50-day: That's not today's spot. Today gave you the trigger and a tight low to risk against.

questions.simple: Buy at market as it clears $21.75 and put your stop a few cents under today's low. That's your spot.
questions.story: It's rested for weeks under the same high, right around $21.75. Today's the buy day.

deeper.counter: Kullamagi says this setup can be traded by anticipating the breakout, but he doesn't find it as effective. We wait for the trigger.

questions.q: Look at the volume on the right side of this base. It dries up. That means buyers are losing interest.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. It's the sellers who are running out, not the buyers. Early in this base the volume bars are tall. On the right side they dry up. The people who wanted out have mostly sold, so fewer shares are for sale. When buyers do show up, price can move. This is LNG in May 2014. The next day it broke out on 3.3x volume and hit 3R the session after. I like seeing volume dry up, and it raises the grade. It's not a must though. A clean base without it still gets bought.
questions.lesson_line: Volume drying up in a base is sellers running out. It raises the grade. It's not a must.
questions.simple: False, it's the sellers drying up, not the buyers. That raises the grade, but it's not a must.

deeper.counter: In our scan of past flat bases, the ones where volume dried up in the second half did about as well as the rest. Bulkowski finds volume trends down inside 70% of rectangles. So it's common, and it's a plus, not a promise.

questions.q: Our card wants a flat base to be the first or second base since the last stage reset.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Our card wants the first or second base since the last stage reset. IBD says it is usually best to buy a first-stage or second-stage base. MarketSmith says third, fourth or later stage bases are late in their moves and may be more likely to fail. The count resets to 1 when price undercuts the prior base's low.
questions.lesson_line: Count the bases. The first two are the ones we want.
questions.simple: True. Our card wants the first or second base, because later bases are late in their move and may fail.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.q: Great sales and earnings growth matter more than what the chart is doing.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The chart comes first. We like growing sales and earnings, and between two good charts I'll take the one with better numbers. But the chart shows you what buyers and sellers are doing right now. It's also where your entry and your stop come from. Great numbers on a broken chart is still a broken chart.
questions.lesson_line: Numbers help you pick. The chart decides.
questions.simple: False, because the chart gives you the entry and the stop, and growth only helps you pick between good charts.

questions.q: Where do you start measuring it from?
choices: The high just before it rested
The lowest low of the whole rest
Where it crossed the 50-day
The day it breaks out
questions.answer: The high just before it rested
questions.why: The high just before it started resting. We call it the left-side high. Everything gets measured from there. How deep the base is, how long it's rested, where the top sits. LII set that high, then spent about three months under it. Get the start wrong and your depth and your pivot are wrong too.
questions.lesson_line: Find the left-side high first. Everything else gets measured from it.

wrong.Where it crossed the 50-day: The 50-day is a line under the base, not where it starts.
wrong.The day it breaks out: That's where the base ends, not where it starts.
wrong.The lowest low of the whole rest: That's the bottom, and you only know it later. The base starts at the high.

questions.simple: Start at the high just before it rested, because the depth and the pivot both get measured from there.
questions.story: The day before the breakout. You want to measure this base: how deep it is and how long.

deeper.counter: MarketSmith calls it the left-side high that began the base, in most cases the highest intraday price of the last 100 days. IBD puts its buy point 10 cents above it.

questions.q: What does that tightness do for your trade?
choices: Keeps your stop close to the buy
Warns you the base is about to fail
Makes the breakout run farther
Lets you buy before the pivot
questions.answer: Keeps your stop close to the buy
questions.why: It keeps your stop close. When the daily ranges get small, the low of the day sits right under the pivot. Your stop goes a few cents under that low, so the risk per share is small. Same dollar risk, more shares. ALLY did exactly this: four taps of 30, inside days into the breakout, and a stop just 1.6% under the buy. Tight doesn't promise a bigger run. It just makes the risk small.
questions.lesson_line: Tight at the end means a close stop. Inside days into the pivot are the picture.

wrong.Makes the breakout run farther: It doesn't promise a bigger run. What it does is keep the risk small.
wrong.Warns you the base is about to fail: Tight is a good sign. The selling has gone quiet right under the top.
wrong.Lets you buy before the pivot: Tight or not, the buy is still the trade through the pivot.

questions.simple: Tight bars put the low of the day near the pivot, so your stop is close and you get more shares.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.story: The day before the breakout. The last two weeks trade in a narrow range, with inside days near the end. An inside day trades inside the day before it.

deeper.counter: IBD says flat bases should show tight trading, and TraderLion wants tight and orderly price action. Same thing we look for.

questions.q: What do those repeated stalls at the top give you?
choices: A clear price to buy the break of
A level to put your stop under
A sign it's about to break down
A reason to buy before it breaks
questions.answer: A clear price to buy the break of
questions.why: A clear price to buy. Every stall is sellers turning the stock back at the same spot, right around 733. So you know exactly where they sit. Set your alert there. When price trades through it, those sellers are done, and that's your buy. Look at today's candle too, a hammer, a little under that high. That's a good look for a buy day. FIX broke out the next day and hit 3R the session after.
questions.lesson_line: A top that holds again and again is the line to watch. The trade through it is the buy.

wrong.A level to put your stop under: The top is where you buy. The stop goes a few cents under the breakout day's low.
wrong.A sign it's about to break down: Stalls at the top don't predict a breakdown. They just mark the price to watch.
wrong.A reason to buy before it breaks: That's guessing. The stalls tell you sellers are still there, so wait for the break.

questions.story: The day before the breakout. This stock has rested about six weeks under 733, and it's run into that same top again and again.
questions.simple: Repeated stalls show you the price where sellers sit, and a trade through it says they're done, so that's your buy.

deeper.counter: IBD draws a line across at least three points along the top. Bulkowski wants one line touched at least three times and the other twice. In our scan, three clean taps did no better than two. So more taps is a cleaner picture, not a must.

questions.q: If the stock closes under its 200-day before the trigger, the flat base is off.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Under the 200-day we don't buy stocks. That's a hard line. A stock under its 200-day is in a downtrend, and a sideways rest down there is a pause in a decline. It's not a leader resting. So a close under it before the trigger ends the setup. The 50-day is different. A quick shakeout under the 50 inside a base is fine.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day there's no flat base to buy. That's a hard line.
questions.simple: True, because under the 200-day a stock is in a downtrend, and we don't buy stocks down there.

deeper.trap: The two lines aren't treated the same. A quick shakeout under the 50-day inside a base is fine. A close under the 200-day ends the setup before it ever triggers.

questions.q: It trades through the pivot and you're 2% over it. It's also 12% above its 9 EMA. Do you buy it?
choices: No, it's too stretched to buy
Yes, it's barely past the pivot
Yes, at half the usual size
Yes, with a tighter stop
questions.answer: No, it's too stretched to buy
questions.why: No. It's too stretched. We skip a long that's more than 10% over its 9 EMA, and this one is 12% over. Being only 2% past the pivot doesn't save it. A stock that far above its average tends to snap back toward it. That drop runs right through a normal stop under the day's low. Half size or a tighter stop doesn't fix a bad entry. I'd let it go and wait for it to tighten up near the 9 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: A breakout that's already stretched is a chase with a different name.

wrong.Yes, it's barely past the pivot: The pivot is the trigger, but the stretch still counts. 12% over the 9 EMA is a chase.
wrong.Yes, at half the usual size: Smaller size on a bad entry is still a bad entry.
wrong.Yes, with a tighter stop: A tighter stop on a stretched stock just gets hit by the snap back.

questions.simple: Skip it, because a stock that far over its 9 EMA can snap back and run right through your stop.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: We never buy a flat base breakout more than ___% above the pivot.
questions.why: 4%. Never buy more than 4% above the buy point. MarketSmith's buy range runs 0% to 5% above the pivot, so our line is stricter. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: Four percent over the pivot and I am done. I would rather miss it than chase it.
questions.simple: The blank is 4, because we never buy more than 4% above the pivot.

deeper.trap: The 5 in the bank is the trap. MarketSmith's range runs to 5% above the pivot, a looser vendor line. Our rulebook cuts it to 4%. Past that, a late buy leaves the stop farther away, so the share count shrinks.

questions.q: Your stop should be a real stop order sitting with your broker, not a price you watch yourself.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Every position gets a real stop order with the broker. A mental stop only works if you're at the screen, and only if you actually sell when it hits. That's exactly when people freeze, or talk themselves into one more day. The order doesn't freeze. Put it in right after you buy, at the price you planned.
questions.lesson_line: A stop in your head is a debate. A stop with the broker is an appointment.
questions.simple: True, because a stop in your head only works if you're watching and willing to sell, and the order just does it.

questions.q: What kind of base are you looking at?
choices: A flat base, one range
A VCP, swings getting smaller
A cup, with a handle forming
A double bottom
questions.answer: A flat base, one range
questions.why: A flat base. It's held one range the whole time, under a level top it's hit five times. A VCP looks different: each pullback is smaller than the one before. A cup drops deeper in a rounded U and then builds a handle. Getting the name right matters, because each one has its own buy point and its own stop.
questions.lesson_line: One range, one ceiling, one floor. That's a flat base.

wrong.A VCP, swings getting smaller: In a VCP each pullback is smaller than the last. These swings stay about the same size.
wrong.A cup, with a handle forming: A cup is a rounded U that drops deeper, then dips again for a handle. This one holds one flat range.
wrong.A double bottom: A double bottom makes two separate lows. This one holds one range under a flat top.

questions.simple: It's a flat base, one range under a level top, and that tells you where the buy point and the stop go.
questions.story: The day before the breakout. About ten weeks sideways, roughly 11% from top to bottom, and the top has been tapped five times.

deeper.counter: IBD says a flat base should look like a rectangular box, no more than 15% deep. A cup falls 12% to 33% in a rounded U before its handle.

questions.q: IBD's buy point is the base's high plus 10 cents; our market order at the trade-through makes the 10 cents moot.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. IBD adds 10 cents to the left-side high for its buy point. We mark the high itself and buy at market as price trades through it. So the 10 cents does not matter to us.
questions.lesson_line: Same level, no 10 cents. The pivot is the high; the trigger is the trade through it.
questions.simple: True. IBD adds 10 cents to its buy point, but our market order as price breaks through makes that gap not matter.

questions.q: The trigger just fired. Do you buy it?
choices: No, earnings are too close
Not today, but buy it Tuesday
Yes, the trigger fired
Yes, but at half size
questions.answer: No, earnings are too close
questions.why: No. Earnings are two days out, and we don't make new buys in the 3 days before a report. The reason is the gap. A report can open the stock way under your stop, and the stop can't catch it. So the loss you planned isn't the loss you get. Let it report. If the setup is still there after, you can trade it then.
questions.lesson_line: A breakout two days before earnings is a coin flip with a story. Let it report.

wrong.Not today, but buy it Tuesday: Tuesday is still inside the 3 days. The window runs right up to the report.
wrong.Yes, the trigger fired: The trigger fired, and the calendar still says no. The earnings window comes first.
wrong.Yes, but at half size: Half size still eats the gap. Smaller is still in.

questions.story: Clean, tight base. It trades through the 112.00 pivot Monday morning. The company reports earnings Wednesday after the close.
questions.simple: No, because a report can gap the stock right past your stop, and this one is only two days away.

deeper.trap: The rule is about the date, not the setup. A clean base, a strong trigger or a smaller size doesn't change it. It covers new buys only. A trade you already own holds through a report only if it's up 5R.

questions.q: Do you sell some here?
choices: Not yet, let it push a few days
Yes, sell a third here at 3R
Yes, sell half and lock it in
Yes, sell it all now, 3R is plenty
questions.answer: Not yet, let it push a few days
questions.why: Not yet. It's only the day after your buy. Today closed red, near its low, and it's a tad extended from the 50-day. After a breakout on that kind of volume, a quiet red day is normal. A real winner runs for several days, and selling this early gives up most of the push. I wait until day 3 at the earliest. Then I sell some into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R. WSM made 5R by day 10. Your stop protects you while it runs.
questions.lesson_line: The first sell is a judgment. Give it until day 3 at least, then sell into the push.

wrong.Yes, sell a third here at 3R: There's no fixed third at 3R. The first sell is a judgment, and this early is almost never the day.
wrong.Yes, sell half and lock it in: Half on day 1 caps your best trades. Let the push play out.
wrong.Yes, sell it all now, 3R is plenty: 3R this fast says it's a leader. Selling it all throws away the run.

questions.simple: Not yet, because a real winner runs for days, and selling on day 1 gives up most of the push.
questions.story: You bought this breakout yesterday. Today it's already up 3R.

questions.q: One R is the fill minus the stop. Where is 3R?
questions.why: 75.92. One R is the fill minus the stop: 73.16 minus 72.24. Add three of those to the fill, 73.16, and you get 75.92. It is a mark on the ruler and not a fixed sell. WSM passed both 3R and 5R on the buy day itself.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. It is a measuring mark, not an automatic sell.
questions.simple: 3R is the fill plus three times the gap between the fill and the stop, which is 75.92.

reasons: computed key: the answer comes from arithmetic on the numbers given

wrong.$75.00: Added the three R to the stop instead of the fill.
wrong.$70.40: Subtracted the three R instead of adding them.

questions.story: Bought on the breakout at 73.16 with the stop at 72.24.

questions.q: A stock rates 85 for RS (how it ranks against other stocks) but sits in one of the weakest groups. It's a leader.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. We want both: an RS rating of 80 or more, and a group that's among the strongest. 85 clears the first bar. The group kills it. When the whole group is being sold, a breakout has nobody behind it. The money is going somewhere else. Leaders come out of the groups that are leading.
questions.lesson_line: A flat base in a laggard group is a box going nowhere. Buy the leaders.
questions.simple: False, because a leader needs a strong group behind it too, and a good rating in a weak group isn't enough.

questions.q: Which ones do you buy?
choices: Just the A+
All three, full size
None, Orange means all cash
The A+ and the A
questions.answer: Just the A+
questions.why: Just the A+. In an Orange market breakouts fail more often, because the market isn't backing them. So I only want my very best idea, the cleanest base with the tightest risk. The A and the B can wait for a better market. Green is when we press. Red is mostly cash.
questions.lesson_line: Read the market before the box. In Orange, only the A+.

wrong.All three, full size: That's how we trade a Green market. Orange narrows it to the A+.
wrong.None, Orange means all cash: Mostly cash is Red. Orange still lets you take your best setup.
wrong.The A+ and the A: Orange is A+ only. The A waits for a better market.

questions.simple: Just the A+, because in a weak market only your cleanest setup is worth the risk.
questions.story: Our market filter in the app has four readings: Green, Yellow, Orange and Red. Today it reads Orange. The market's under pressure, one step from Red. Three flat bases trigger this morning. One is an A+, our cleanest kind of setup, the kind we size up on. One is an A, one a B.

questions.q: The floor broke and came right back. What's the trade now?
choices: The reclaim, as its own setup
The breakout through the old top
Nothing, the stock is broken
A short, stop just over 71
questions.answer: The reclaim, as its own setup
questions.why: The reclaim. Once it undercut the floor, the flat base was over. But it took 71 back in two days. That's a shakeout. The dip flushed out weak holders, and buyers stepped right back in. We call it an undercut and reclaim, a U&R. It's its own trade, with its own trigger and its own stop. How fast a reclaim has to come is a judgment call. Two days is quick.
questions.lesson_line: Lose the floor and the box is gone. A fast reclaim is its own trade.

wrong.The breakout through the old top: The undercut ended the flat base. The old top isn't this trade's trigger anymore.
wrong.Nothing, the stock is broken: A quick reclaim is a shakeout, not a break. It's a different setup, not no setup.
wrong.A short, stop just over 71: It took the floor back in two days. Shorting that is fighting the buyers who just showed up.

questions.story: A nine-week flat base has a floor at 71. Tuesday it undercuts it, with a low of 70.40. Thursday it closes back above 71.
questions.simple: The trade is the reclaim, because the undercut ended the flat base and buyers took the floor back fast.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.q: Tap the words that fit the blank.
questions.sentence: The ___ is not the stop; it can sit a whole base's depth away.
questions.answer: base low
questions.why: The base low. It is not the stop, and it can be up to 15% away, the base's depth. That breaks our rule that the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy. The stop is a few cents under the breakout day's low.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is the breakout day's low, not the bottom of the box.
questions.simple: The base low is not the stop, because it can sit up to 15% away, far wider than our usual stop.

deeper.trap: Two mistakes are named on the card. One is putting the stop at the base low, which is too wide. The other is pulling the stop tighter just to fit the size. Neither is the fix. The stop is a few cents under the breakout day's low.

questions.q: The lowest low in the two months before the base was 40.00 and the left-side high is 50.00. The prior advance, in percent?
questions.why: 25%. The advance is the gain from the lowest low to the left-side high, divided by the low. 50 minus 40 is 10, and 10 over 40 is 25%. IBD looks for a prior uptrend of at least 30% in price. Kullamagi looks for a move of 30% to 100% or more in the past 1 to 3 months. A 25% run is under both lines.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the run before the rest. A box with no run in front of it is just a box.
questions.simple: The run is the gain from the low to the high, divided by the low, which is 25% here.

reasons: computed key: the answer comes from arithmetic on the numbers given

wrong.20%: Divided the gain by the high instead of the low.
wrong.125%: Forgot to subtract one: the high as a percent of the low.
wrong.10%: Read the 10 points of gain as 10 percent.

questions.q: Left-side high 100.00, the base's lowest intraday low 86.50. How deep is the base, in percent?
questions.why: 13.5%. Depth is the left-side high minus the base's lowest intraday low, divided by the high: 100 minus 86.5, over 100. MarketSmith measures it that way. IBD says a flat base declines no more than 15% from its intraday peak to its intraday trough.
questions.lesson_line: Depth is high to low, divided by the high. Measure it; do not eyeball it.
questions.simple: Depth is the drop from the high to the low as a share of the high, which is 13.5% here.

reasons: computed key: the answer comes from arithmetic on the numbers given

wrong.15.6%: Divided the drop by the low instead of the high.
wrong.86.5%: Took the low as a percent of the high and skipped the drop.
wrong.1.4%: Decimal slip: moved the decimal one place.

questions.q: How far below your fill is that stop, in percent?
questions.why: 2.08%. The gap is 72.20 minus 70.70, which is 1.50. Divide that by your fill: 1.50 divided by 72.20 is 2.08%. That's right where I like it, inside 1 to 3%. The math matters because the distance sets your size. Same dollar risk, a closer stop buys more shares and a wider one buys fewer. This was APH, and it went on to hit 3R on day 3.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.
questions.simple: Your stop is 2.08% under the fill, inside the 1 to 3% I like, and that distance sets your size.

deeper.example: APH, 2026-01-12: bought at 72.20 with the stop at 70.70, 2.1% away. It hit 3R on day 3 and ran to 7.6R. The stop came from the day's low first. The size came after.

reasons: computed key: the answer comes from arithmetic on the numbers given

wrong.1.50%: That's the dollar gap, 1.50, read as a percent. Divide it by the fill.
wrong.20.80%: Decimal slip. The real answer is ten times smaller.
wrong.0.02%: That's the ratio. Multiply by 100 to get the percent.

questions.story: You bought the breakout at 72.20. Your stop is a few cents under the low of the day, at 70.70.

questions.q: How many R are you up?
questions.answer: 5R
questions.why: 5R. One R is your risk per share, the fill minus the stop: 30.28 minus 29.79. Your gain is 32.73 minus 30.28. Divide the gain by one R and you get 5. We count in R because it puts every trade on the same ruler, whatever the price or the size. Our rules run on it. The stop can move up to breakeven between 2R and 5R. You only hold through earnings when you're up 5R.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R, not dollars. Every trade on the same ruler.
questions.simple: The gain is five times your risk per share, so you're up 5R, and R is how we compare every trade.

5R
