questions.story: You bought the breakout at 30.28 with your stop at 29.79. A few weeks later it trades up to 32.73.

questions.q: Your stop hasn't been hit yet. What do you do?
choices: Hold, the stop is still the exit
Sell at tomorrow's open, it failed
Move the stop under the base low
Buy more, it's cheaper now
questions.answer: Hold, the stop is still the exit
questions.why: Hold it. Your stop is the exit, and you set it before the trade, when you were thinking clearly. A close back inside the base is a warning. It's not an exit by itself. Don't sell early on a feeling, and never give it more room. In this case the warning was right. AMZN's next session hit 176.75 and took the 178.10 stop. A small, planned loss. That's the system working.
questions.lesson_line: A weak close is a warning. The stop is the decision, and you made it before you bought.

wrong.Sell at tomorrow's open, it failed: A weak close is a warning, not an exit. The stop is the exit, and it's already set.
wrong.Move the stop under the base low: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.Buy more, it's cheaper now: Never add to a trade that's flashing a warning. A weak close isn't a discount.

questions.story: You bought this breakout with a stop at 178.10. By the close it's given it all back. It closes at 178.15, the low of the day, back inside the base.
questions.simple: Hold, because your stop was set with a clear head before the trade, and one weak close is only a warning.

deeper.example: This is AMZN. The breakout day closed at 178.15, the low of its range, on 0.72x volume. The next session's low of 176.75 took the 178.10 stop. The weak close was the warning. The stop did the exit, as planned.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Buy at market, stop under the day's low
Buy at market, stop at the base low
Buy at market, stop pulled in to fit
Pass; any buy past the pivot is a chase
questions.answer: Buy at market, stop under the day's low
questions.why: Buy. 91.80 is inside our chase line: never buy more than 4% above the buy point. The stop stays a few cents under the breakout day's low. The base low is too wide, and pulling the stop in to fit the size is also a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: Late is not too late. Inside the chase line, buy, and keep the stop under the day's low.

wrong.Buy at market, stop at the base low: The base low is not the stop. It can sit a whole base's depth away. The stop is a few cents under the breakout day's low.
wrong.Buy at market, stop pulled in to fit: Pulling the stop tighter to fit the size is a named mistake. The stop comes first and the size comes from it.
wrong.Pass; any buy past the pivot is a chase: The chase line is more than 4% above the buy point, not any price past it. 91.80 is inside the line.

questions.story: The pivot is 90.00. You missed the open. At 10:15 the stock trades 91.80.
questions.simple: Buy at market with the stop under the day's low, because 91.80 is inside the chase line.

deeper.trap: Passing feels safe, but the rule is a line, not a ban on late buys. Past 4% you skip it. Inside it you buy, and the stop stays under the day's low. Chasing costs size: the stop stays put, the distance grows and the shares shrink.

reasons: computed key: the answer comes from arithmetic on the numbers given

questions.q: Where's your stop now?
choices: 50.30, the first 30-minute low
50.95, the first 30-minute high
Sell it all at the open, 50.60
Out now, the loss is past 2R
questions.answer: 50.30, the first 30-minute low
questions.why: 50.30, the low of the first 30 minutes. Your stop can't catch a gap. The stock just opened past it. So we let the first 30 minutes decide. That low becomes the new stop, because it shows where buyers stepped in. There's a ceiling. If those 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, you get out. Your risk was 52.00 down to 51.00. Down to 50.30 is less than twice that, so the low stands.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through your stop is the one exception. The first 30 minutes decide.

wrong.50.95, the first 30-minute high: The new stop is the low of that first bar, not the high.
wrong.Sell it all at the open, 50.60: The open isn't the decision. The first 30 minutes are.
wrong.Out now, the loss is past 2R: It isn't. Down to 50.30 is less than twice your 52.00 to 51.00 risk.

questions.story: You bought at 52.00 with your stop at 51.00. It gaps down and opens at 50.60, under your stop. The first 30 minutes trade between 50.30 and 50.95.
questions.simple: The new stop is 50.30, the first 30-minute low, because that's where buyers stepped in and you're still inside 2R.

deeper.trap: A stop only moves up, never down or wider. The gap rule is the one exception. That's why the new stop, 50.30, sits under the old one at 51.00.

reasons: computed key: the answer comes from arithmetic on the numbers given

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Set the alert at the ___ and buy as price trades through it in regular hours.
questions.answer: pivot
questions.why: The pivot. Alert at the pivot, market order as it trades through, regular hours only.
questions.lesson_line: Alert at the pivot. Then the market comes to you.

questions.q: A tight base has a 44.00 pivot and sits at 43.20 on an inside day. Buying it now, before the trade-through, is a named mistake on our card.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The trigger is the trade through the pivot in regular hours, here 44.00. Anticipating inside the base with no trigger is a named mistake on our card. Kullamagi finds anticipating the breakout less effective. An inside day shows the base is tight. It is not the buy.
questions.lesson_line: Feeling it coming is not a trigger. The pivot is.
questions.simple: Buying before the trade-through is anticipating, and the buy is the move through 44.00.

questions.q: On a normal day with no gap, a flat base trade that trades down to its stop is sold at the stop.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule, which does not apply on a normal day. When price trades down to it, the exit is taken.
questions.lesson_line: My stop is my stop. That is the whole rule.
questions.simple: True. The stop is the exit, so on a normal day you sell when price reaches it and do not move it wider.

questions.q: It's back where you bought it. What do you do?
choices: Hold, the stop stays at 72.24
Lower the stop to give it room
Sell it, the breakout failed
Raise the stop to the pivot
questions.answer: Hold, the stop stays at 72.24
questions.why: Hold it. This is normal. Two in three breakouts like this come back to the breakout price within 30 days. Your stop is 72.24, and that's the only line that says you're wrong. Selling here, or lowering the stop, swaps a plan you made calmly for a feeling. Raising it to the pivot is no better. Then normal noise takes you out of a good trade.
questions.lesson_line: The retest is normal. Your stop pays for it. You don't widen it.

wrong.Raise the stop to the pivot: A stop right on the pivot sits in the noise and invites a shakeout. Nothing here says to move it.
wrong.Lower the stop to give it room: The stop never moves down or wider. 72.24 is the line.
wrong.Sell it, the breakout failed: A test of the pivot isn't a failure. Most breakouts do it. The stop decides.

questions.story: You bought the breakout at 73.16. Three days later it slides back to the pivot at 73.00. Your stop is 72.24.
questions.simple: Hold, because most breakouts come back to test the pivot, and only your stop says the trade is wrong.

deeper.example: WSM reached 5R by day 10. Then in late October it came back to 71.56, through the pivot and the original stop. That's the two-in-three throwback in person. The stop isn't widened for it. A new buy needs a new trigger and its own stop.

questions.q: Your flat base breakout is working. When do you move the stop up to breakeven?
choices: Between 2R and 5R
Between 0.5R and 1R
Between 1R and 1.5R
Between 6R and 8R
questions.answer: Between 2R and 5R
questions.why: Between 2R and 5R, or when you make your first sell. It's a judgment, not a fixed spot. Move it too early, like at 1R, and a normal pullback to the pivot stops you out for nothing. Two in three breakouts like this come back to the breakout price within 30 days. Wait too long and a big winner can turn into a loser. Somewhere in that 2R to 5R window, it's your call.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven somewhere between 2R and 5R, or at your first sell. A judgment, not a fixed spot.

wrong.Between 0.5R and 1R: Too early. A normal pullback to the pivot stops you out at breakeven, then it runs without you.
wrong.Between 6R and 8R: Too late. By then a winner can come all the way back and turn into a loss.
wrong.Between 1R and 1.5R: Still too early. Breakouts test the pivot all the time, and that takes you out.

questions.simple: Between 2R and 5R, because earlier a normal pullback stops you out, and later a winner can turn into a loser.

questions.q: Your breakout is only up 0.6R after 12 trading days. You sell it and move on.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. That's our time stop. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days gets sold. This one's had 12 days and it's at 0.6R. A real leader doesn't sit around that long after a breakout. Meanwhile your money's stuck in it, and it could be in something that's working. You don't wait for the stop. You sell it and free the money.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and nothing. The money has somewhere better to be.
questions.simple: True, because a trade stuck under 1R after 10 days isn't working, and that money can go to a better setup.

questions.q: Do you sell some at the open?
choices: Your call, either way is fine
Yes, a gap past 3R is a must-sell
Yes, sell it all into the gap
No, never sell on a gap day
questions.answer: Your call, either way is fine
questions.why: It's your call. A gap past 3R isn't an automatic sell. Selling some into it locks in a good gain at a strong price. Holding keeps you in a stock that's clearly working. Both are fine. It's day 4, so you're past the day 3 mark where I'd start thinking about selling. Whatever you pick, keep the stop where it is.
questions.lesson_line: A gap past 3R is a chance, not an order. Selling some is your call.

wrong.Yes, a gap past 3R is a must-sell: No gap is a must-sell. Selling some is a judgment call, never a rule.
wrong.Yes, sell it all into the gap: Selling it all throws away a stock that's working. If you sell, sell some and trail the rest.
wrong.No, never sell on a gap day: You're allowed to. Selling some into a big gap is a fair choice.

questions.story: Your flat base long is on day 4. It closed Thursday at 2.6R. Friday it gaps open to 3.4R.
questions.simple: Your call, because a gap is a chance to bank some gain or keep riding a stock that's working.

deeper.example: It opened past 3R on day 4, so selling some is fair. So is holding it all and trailing. Either way, the stop stays.

questions.q: Your normal size doesn't fit that stop. What do you do?
choices: Fewer shares, stop stays at the low
Move the stop up so the size fits
Full size, it's only one trade
Use a 7% stop to give it room
questions.answer: Fewer shares, stop stays at the low
questions.why: Fewer shares. Your stop goes a few cents under 46.40, the low of the day. That's where the chart says you're wrong. About 4.5% is wider than I like, but under 5% I'll take it. The size comes from the stop, never the other way around. Pull the stop up just to fit more shares and normal noise takes you out of a good trade. So you buy fewer shares, or you wait for a tighter entry.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, size second. Never move the stop to fit the size.

wrong.Move the stop up so the size fits: That's the mistake. The stop now sits in the noise, not where the chart says you're wrong.
wrong.Full size, it's only one trade: Full size on a 4.5% stop is a bigger loss than you planned. The size comes from the stop.
wrong.Use a 7% stop to give it room: That's past the 5% we'll take, and the low of the day is your stop anyway.

questions.story: You bought the breakout at 48.60. The low of the day is 46.40, about 4.5% under your fill.
questions.simple: Fewer shares, because the stop goes where the chart says you're wrong and the size comes from the stop.

deeper.trap: The trap is sizing first. You pick the size you want, then pick a tight stop that makes the math work. Now the stop isn't where the chart puts it. The honest stop comes first. Past 5%, we mostly wait for a tighter trigger.

reasons: owner rulebook A3/A4 (stop first, stop never moves wider)
held decision D-005 (what to do when the honest stop is wider than usual) is not keyed: the choices carry no stop percent

questions.q: Clean flat base, but it's the fourth base since this run started. What does that tell you?
choices: It's late in the move, riskier
It's proven, so it's safer
Nothing, base count doesn't matter
It's early, lots of room to run
questions.answer: It's late in the move, riskier
questions.why: It's late in the move, and late bases fail more. By a fourth base, everyone has seen this stock. Plenty of early buyers are sitting on big gains, ready to sell. A clean shape doesn't change where it sits in the run. I want first and second bases. That's where the big moves start. The count goes back to 1 if price undercuts the prior base's low.
questions.lesson_line: A clean box on the fourth floor is still the fourth floor.

wrong.It's proven, so it's safer: A long run means it's late, not safe. Late-stage breakouts often blow up.
wrong.Nothing, base count doesn't matter: It matters. First and second bases are where the big moves come from.
wrong.It's early, lots of room to run: Backwards. A fourth base comes after three others, so the move is late.

questions.simple: It's late in the move, so it's more likely to fail, and a clean shape doesn't change that.

deeper.counter: IBD says breakouts from late-stage bases will often blow up, and it's usually best to buy a first or second-stage base. MarketSmith says third, fourth or later stage bases are late in their moves and may be more likely to fail.
deeper.trap: The trap is a beautiful box. A fourth base can look like a perfect rectangle and still sit late in the move. Shape and stage are two separate checks.

reasons: card base-count line is proposed and the owner may want a third base graded B- instead of a pass
MarketSmith wording is hedged (may be more likely)

questions.q: You're stopped out. What did that stop just do for you?
choices: Its job, a small planned loss
Cost you, it needed more room
Saved you from any loss at all
Proved the setup was bad
questions.answer: Its job, a small planned loss
questions.why: Its job. You bought at 241.28 and the stop at 236.86 took you out on day 1, a planned loss of 1.83%. Then look what came next. Two sessions later it closed at 216.08, 10% under your fill. Give it room and you're in a 14% hole in three sessions. A stop hit is still a loss, and one stop-out says nothing about the setup. That's the cost of being there for the ones that work.
questions.lesson_line: A loss taken at your stop is the system working.

wrong.Cost you, it needed more room: More room was a 14% hole in three sessions. The stop saved you most of that.
wrong.Saved you from any loss at all: A stop hit is still a loss. It kept the loss small.
wrong.Proved the setup was bad: One stop-out doesn't judge a setup. The next trigger is a new trade.

questions.story: You bought the gap open at 241.28, above the pivot. It closes mid-range on average volume. Next day the low hits your stop at 236.86.
questions.simple: It did its job, because it cut a small planned loss before the stock fell a lot further.

deeper.example: META, 2020-06-23: bought at 241.28 with the stop at 236.86, 1.83% under the fill. Stopped on day 1, and it never showed a gain. It only got back to the pivot about six weeks later.

reasons: owner rulebook A4 (the stop is the exit)

questions.q: Which one do you grade higher?
choices: The 1.9x day closing at the high
The 0.8x day, quiet is better
Same grade, only the pivot matters
Neither, skip anything under 2x
questions.answer: The 1.9x day closing at the high
questions.why: The 1.9x day that closes at the high. Heavy volume means a lot of buyers took the shares. A close at the high means they held on into the bell. That's real demand. In our scan of past flat bases, breakouts on 1.4x volume or more hit 3R 39.2% of the time. Below 1.4x it was 26.0%. Still, volume only raises the grade. The quiet one can still be bought, just smaller.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy volume and a close at the high make the stronger day. Volume raises the grade.

wrong.The 0.8x day, quiet is better: Quiet is what you want inside the base. At the breakout you want a crowd.
wrong.Same grade, only the pivot matters: The pivot is the trigger. Volume and the close are what raise the grade.
wrong.Neither, skip anything under 2x: There's no 2x bar. Volume raises the grade. It doesn't decide the buy.

questions.story: Same base, two different breakouts. We grade every setup A+, A, B or B-, and the grade sets your size. One breakout trades through on 0.8x its 50-day average volume and closes mid-range. The other trades through on 1.9x and closes at the high.
questions.simple: The heavy-volume day closing at the high, because it shows buyers took the shares and held them into the close.

reasons: held decision D-006 (is breakout volume a grade cue or a gate) is on a provisional default

deeper.counter: IBD wants breakout volume at least 40% to 50% above average. TraderLion says 1.4 times. Our scan agrees it helps. It just isn't a must.

questions.q: What is the read?
choices: Wide and loose; the base is off
Still a flat base; the top holds
It will tighten; the base stays on
Fine; only the depth matters here
questions.answer: Wide and loose; the base is off
questions.why: Wide and loose, so the base is off. Our test: the average daily range of the last 10 sessions is larger than that of the base's first 10 sessions. The story has exactly that, so a flat top does not save it. A box that gets louder as it goes is unwinding, not resting.
questions.lesson_line: A box that gets louder as it goes is not resting. It is unwinding.

wrong.Still a flat base; the top holds: A flat top over widening bars is a ragged box. The ranges are the tell.
wrong.It will tighten; the base stays on: Hope is not a setup. The test is the ranges now, and the last 10 sessions are wider than the first 10.
wrong.Fine; only the depth matters here: Depth is one test. Our card also checks the ranges, and the last 10 sessions are wider than the first 10.

questions.story: Six weeks into a base, the daily bars have grown. The last ten sessions swing wider every day than the first ten did. The top is still flat.
questions.simple: The daily swings keep growing, so this is not a calm rest and we call the base off.

reasons: card criterion is proposed (the owner reviews it)

questions.q: What's the 50-day telling you here?
choices: The trend is intact, it's resting
It's weak, the line breaks soon
Nothing, only the 200-day line counts
Buy now, before the pivot
questions.answer: The trend is intact, it's resting
questions.why: The trend's intact. It's resting, not breaking down. The 50-day is the medium-term trend. FIX ran from about 300 to the 733 area, and through this whole rest it held above a steep, rising 50-day. Nobody's dumping it. A stock that closes under its 50 and lives there is falling, not resting. A quick dip under it is fine. Living under it isn't.
questions.lesson_line: A leader rests above its rising 50-day. A stock living under it is falling, not resting.

wrong.It's weak, the line breaks soon: A rising line under price is support. Weak is a stock that closes under it and stays.
wrong.Nothing, only the 200-day line counts: The 200-day is our hard line. The 50-day shows the trend your swing rides on.
wrong.Buy now, before the pivot: A good-looking rest isn't a trigger. You still buy the trade through the pivot.

questions.story: The day before the breakout. This stock has rested for weeks after a big run. Check where price sits against its 50-day.
questions.simple: The trend is intact, because a stock resting above a rising 50-day hasn't given back its run.

reasons: card criterion is proposed (the owner reviews it)

deeper.counter: Kullamagi says that in the consolidation price surfs the rising 10- and 20-day and sometimes toes the 50-day.

questions.q: Your account is $50,000 and you risk 0.5% on this one. How many shares do you buy?
questions.answer: 173 shares
questions.why: 173 shares. Start with the dollars you're willing to lose: 0.5% of $50,000. Then the risk per share: 59.40 minus 57.96. Divide the dollars by the risk per share and round down. That's 173. Now if the stop hits, you lose what you planned, no more. That's the whole point. The stop decides the size, so a loss at the stop always costs the same slice of your account.
questions.lesson_line: The stop sets the size. Dollar risk divided by the gap, rounded down.
questions.simple: Divide the dollars you'll risk by the gap to your stop, round down to 173, and a stop-out costs what you planned.

deeper.trap: The trap is rounding up. Round up and you risk a little more than you chose. The other slip is dividing by the price instead of the gap to the stop.

choices: 347 shares
1,736 shares
173 shares
4 shares

wrong.347 shares: That's double. You doubled the risk percent.
wrong.1,736 shares: Decimal slip. Your risk dollars came out ten times too big.
wrong.4 shares: You divided by the price, 59.40, instead of the gap to your stop.

questions.story: You bought the breakout at 59.40. Your stop is 57.96, a few cents under the low of the day.

questions.q: You're trailing what's left of a winner on the 9 EMA. The first time price touches the line, you sell.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. You sell on a close below the line, not a touch. Price can dip under the 9 EMA during the day and finish back above it. That's noise. A close under it means the selling held all day, and the push is over. Fast movers trail the 9 EMA. Steadier ones trail the 20. Either way, the close decides.
questions.lesson_line: Trail the rising average. Sell the close below it, not the touch.
questions.simple: False, because a dip under the line can bounce back by the close. Only a close below it shows the selling held.

reasons: owner rulebook E52 (trail and close-below rule)

deeper.counter: Kullamagi's beginner rule waits for the first close below his 10-day. Same idea: the close, not the touch.

questions.q: Do you take it?
choices: No, it's too cheap and too thin
No, but only because it's under $10
Yes, the base is clean
Yes, but at half size
questions.answer: No, it's too cheap and too thin
questions.why: No. We only trade stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. This one's $7 and does about $4 million. It fails both. Thin stocks are hard to get out of. When your stop hits, there may be no buyers at that price, and you sell well under it. A clean base doesn't fix that. We don't even watch names like this.
questions.lesson_line: A clean box in a thin stock is still a thin stock.

wrong.No, but only because it's under $10: The $4 million a day misses the $20 million floor too. It fails both.
wrong.Yes, the base is clean: The chart is fine. The stock isn't ours. Liquidity comes before the chart.
wrong.Yes, but at half size: Half size doesn't make a thin stock easy to sell.

questions.story: A clean flat base triggers this morning. The stock is $7 and trades about $4 million a day.
questions.simple: No, because a cheap thin stock is hard to sell at your stop, and a clean chart doesn't fix that.

reasons: key rests on one rulebook fact (B23)

questions.q: The stock trades 2,000,000 shares a day on average. What's the most shares you'd ever own?
choices: 20,000 shares
40,000 shares
200,000 shares
No cap if the stop is tight
questions.answer: 20,000 shares
questions.why: 20,000 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume. 1% of 2,000,000 is 20,000. Own more than that and getting out fast becomes a problem. Your own selling pushes the price down. A tight stop doesn't change it. Your risk-based size still has to fit under this ceiling.
questions.lesson_line: One percent of the daily volume, and not a share more.

wrong.200,000 shares: That's ten times our line. The ceiling is 1% of the daily volume.
wrong.40,000 shares: That's double our line. The ceiling is 1% of the daily volume.
wrong.No cap if the stop is tight: A tight stop doesn't lift the cap. Getting out is the problem, not the stop.

questions.simple: 20,000 shares, because we never own more than 1% of the daily volume, so we can always get out fast.

reasons: key rests on one rulebook fact (D42)

questions.q: What is it?
choices: A cup with a handle
A flat base
A high tight flag
A double bottom
questions.answer: A cup with a handle
questions.why: A cup with a handle. A flat base stays boxy and falls 15% or less. This one fell 24% in a rounded U, climbed back near the high, then dipped just under it. That last dip is the handle. IBD and MarketSmith both cap the flat base at 15% deep. It is not a high tight flag, because that needs a pole that nearly doubles and this run was 60%. Our card has a cup falling 12% to 33%.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the depth. Past the box, it is a cup, with its own rules.

wrong.A flat base: 24% is past every flat base line. The U shape says cup as well.
wrong.A high tight flag: A flag needs a pole that nearly doubles and a short pause. This is a long rounded fall.
wrong.A double bottom: The story is one rounded fall and a climb back, not two separate lows.

questions.story: The stock ran 60% into a high, then fell 24% over ten weeks in a rounded U. It climbed back near the high. Now it dips a few percent just under the high.
questions.simple: It is a cup with a handle, because a flat base never falls past 15% and this one fell 24%.

deeper.trap: The trap is judging by the look. A rounded base near the high can feel flat. Measure it. IBD and MarketSmith stop a flat base at 15%, and this one is 24% deep. The small dip at the end is not a flat base tightening. It is the handle before the buy.

reasons: held decision D-043 (flat base depth) is not keyed: 24% is past every option
the card's cup range of 12% to 33% is narrower than MarketSmith's, so only the 24% is keyed

questions.q: What is it?
choices: A high tight flag
A flat base
A cup with handle
A VCP, shrinking pullbacks
questions.answer: A high tight flag
questions.why: A high tight flag. The stock doubled in six weeks, which is the pole. Then it paused in a tight range near the top. Our card says a high tight flag nearly doubles first, then pauses a few weeks. A flat base is a longer rest after a smaller run. The 8% depth does not name it. The run does.
questions.lesson_line: Doubled and paused is a flag. Ran and rested for weeks is a box.

wrong.A flat base: The doubling pole names the setup. A flat base follows a smaller run and rests longer.
wrong.A cup with handle: No rounded fall here. A tight shelf on top of a pole is the flag.
wrong.A VCP, shrinking pullbacks: A VCP needs pullbacks that shrink one after another. This is one tight pause on top of a pole.

questions.story: The stock doubled in six weeks on news, then paused twelve sessions in a tight range near the top. The pause is 8% deep.
questions.simple: A pole that nearly doubles and a short pause on top is a high tight flag, not a flat base.

deeper.trap: The pause is only 8% deep, which looks like a flat base. Depth does not separate the two setups. The run does. A flat base follows a smaller run, around 30%, and a flag follows a pole that nearly doubles. Writers differ a little on the exact pole size, but a stock that doubled in six weeks clears every version.

reasons: held decision D-042 (flat base minimum length) is not keyed
the card's flag pole size is stricter than some public write-ups, so the pole is not keyed on a number

questions.q: Look at the dip in the last 27 sessions. What kind of base is this?
choices: A cup-shaped base, a rounded dip
A flat base with a level floor
A high tight flag on a big pole
A V-shaped bottom after a crash
questions.answer: A cup-shaped base, a rounded dip
questions.why: A cup-shaped base. A flat base is shallow and boxy: IBD says it should look like a rectangular box with a correction of no more than 15%. This one dipped 18.5% from the left-side high in a rounded U, so it is cup-shaped, with its own rules, and not a flat base. The three taps of the top and the 51% run before it do not change the shape. In our scan it reached 1.1R and was stopped.
questions.lesson_line: A flat base is shallow and boxy. A deeper, rounded dip is a cup.

wrong.A flat base with a level floor: A flat base is shallow and boxy, and this dip is deeper and rounded. Three taps of the top do not make a box.
wrong.A high tight flag on a big pole: A flag needs a pole that nearly doubles, and this run was 51%.
wrong.A V-shaped bottom after a crash: A V comes after a crash. This stock ran up 51% first and then rested.

questions.story: The day before a breakout. The stock ran 51% and then rested for 27 sessions, tapping the same top three times. Look at the shape of the rest.
questions.simple: A flat base is a shallow box, and this rest fell deeper in a rounded U, so it is a cup shape.

deeper.trap: The trap is counting taps first. Three clean taps of the top feel like a flat base, so you stop looking at the shape. Look at how deep and how round the dip is first. This one fell 18.5% from the left-side high after a 51% run, deeper than the 15% that IBD allows a flat base.

reasons: held decision D-043 (flat base depth) is not keyed: 18.5% is past every option
the 18.5% is our scan's own number

questions.q: Take it as a flat base?
choices: No; the 50-day is under the 200-day
Yes; price is above both
Yes; the 50 is close enough
questions.answer: No; the 50-day is under the 200-day
questions.why: No. Our card wants the close above the 50-day and the 200-day with the 50 above the 200. A base built in a recovery out of a downtrend is not a leader resting. It worked, and it is still not ours.
questions.lesson_line: Price above both lines is half the check. The 50 over the 200 is the other half.

wrong.Yes; price is above both: Price above both with the 50 under the 200 is a recovery, not a leader's rest.
wrong.Yes; the 50 is close enough: Close enough is under. The order of the lines is the rule.

questions.story: A 28-session base after a 42% rebound out of a downtrend. On the breakout day the close is 14% above the 200-day, but the 50-day still sits 1.6% under the 200-day.

questions.q: The trend line through the closes rises 4% of their average from start to end. That still counts as flat on our card.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Flat means the line through the base's closes moves no more than 10% of the base's average close from start to end. A 4% drift is inside that. A slight U shape inside that drift is allowed too. IBD says a flat base can have a U shape and not look so flat. The test uses the closes, not the lows.
questions.lesson_line: Flat is a ceiling and a small drift, not a ruler.
questions.simple: True, because a drift of 4% is well inside the 10% that our card allows.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading flat as level. The test is a trend line through the closes, so a slight slope or a shallow U passes. Judge the drift against the average close, not by eye.

reasons: card criterion is proposed (the 10% drift is a card number)

questions.q: What was the lesson?
choices: A stop inside the noise gets shaken out
Never buy on heavy volume
Widen the next stop to the base low
Skip breakouts that gap down
questions.answer: A stop inside the noise gets shaken out
questions.why: A stop inside the stock's normal daily range gets shaken out by noise. You never pull a stop in to fit; and the re-entry on the reclaim is a new trade with its own stop.
questions.lesson_line: A stop that sits inside a normal day is not a stop. It is a coin flip.

wrong.Never buy on heavy volume: Volume was not the problem. The stop's distance was.
wrong.Widen the next stop to the base low: The base low is too far the other way. The honest stop is the day's low, judged against the range.
wrong.Skip breakouts that gap down: The gap came after the buy. The lesson is about where the stop sat.

questions.story: Breakout on heavy volume, but it closes near the day's low. Your stop sits 0.88% under the fill while the stock's average daily range is 2.5%. Next morning a 2% gap down takes the stop; then it reclaims the pivot and runs.

questions.q: Bought at 73.16, stop 72.24. Where is 5R?
questions.why: 77.76. One R is the fill minus the stop; five of those above the fill. WSM got there by day 10, then threw back through the pivot.
questions.lesson_line: Know 5R before the open too. The second third comes off there.

questions.q: What do you do with the rest?
choices: Sell it, it closed under the trail
Hold, the stop is at breakeven
Hold until it closes under the base
Hold, the trail is only a guide
questions.answer: Sell it, it closed under the trail
questions.why: Sell it. What's left trails the 9 EMA if it's a fast mover, or the 20 EMA if it's steadier. The exit is a close under that line, and you just got one. That close says the push is over. Breakeven is your floor, not your exit. You'd give back the whole move waiting for it. APH later fell back through the base to 63.10. The sells and the trail kept it a winner.
questions.lesson_line: Part banked, the rest on the trail. The close under the line is the exit.

wrong.Hold, the stop is at breakeven: Breakeven is the floor, not the plan. The trail is the exit for what's left.
wrong.Hold until it closes under the base: That gives back most of the move. The trail line is much closer.
wrong.Hold, the trail is only a guide: The trail is the exit for what's left. A close under it means sell.

questions.story: You bought at 72.20, stop 70.70. It hits 3R on day three and 5R by day ten. You sold some into each push. Then it rolls over and closes below its trail line.
questions.simple: Sell what's left, because a close under your trail line says the push is over.

deeper.example: APH, 2026-01-12: bought at 72.20 with the stop at 70.70. 3R on day 3, 5R by day 10, then it failed back through the base with a low of 63.10. Selling into the pushes and trailing the rest kept it a win.

reasons: owner rulebook E52 (which trail line fits which stock)
the story does not say whether the stock is fast or steady; both lines break on a close below

questions.q: You took the loss at your stop. Was the trade a mistake?
choices: No, a planned loss on a weak day
Yes, you should've sold at 1.63R
No, but widen the stop next time
Yes, light volume meant skip it
questions.answer: No, a planned loss on a weak day
questions.why: No. You bought the trigger with your stop a few cents under the low of the day. You took the loss where you planned. That's the system working. Light volume lowers the grade. It doesn't cancel the trade. LII broke out on 0.82x volume and still ran to 15.9R. And 1.63R was never a place to sell. We wait for a push of several days. Small planned losses are the cost of being there for the ones that run.
questions.lesson_line: Light volume lowers the grade, not the rule. A loss at your stop is the plan working.

wrong.No, but widen the stop next time: The stop only moves up, never wider. Under the low of the day is right.
wrong.Yes, you should've sold at 1.63R: Selling at 1.63R is fear, not a plan. The first sell waits for a push of several days.
wrong.Yes, light volume meant skip it: Volume only raises the grade. Light volume lowers it. It doesn't cancel the trade.

questions.story: A clean six-week shelf, four taps, and volume that dries up in the base. You buy at market at 206.85 as it trades through the pivot, stop 203.95. By the close, volume is only 0.5x and it sits low in its range. It reaches 1.63R, then the stop is hit on day six.
questions.simple: No, because the loss was small and planned, and light volume only lowers the grade.

deeper.trap: The trap is hindsight. The trade lost, so the weak volume looks like the cause. But volume only raises the grade, so the setup still counted. Judge the process: entry, stop and size all followed the rules.

reasons: held decision D-006 (volume as a gate or a cue) is on a provisional default

questions.q: It's still pushing. How do you plan your selling from here?
choices: Sell some into a 3, 5 or 7 day push
Sell nothing, just trail the stop up
Sell a third here, at 3R
Sell it all when it hits 5R
questions.answer: Sell some into a 3, 5 or 7 day push
questions.why: Sell some into the push. The first sell is a judgment. It's not a fixed third at 3R. You're on day 5, past the day 3 mark, and it's running. That's when I start selling some into strength, into a 3, 5 or 7 day push or at about 5 to 10R. Then trail the rest. BAC made 5R in about three weeks, then fell back into the base. The sells on the way up kept that gain.
questions.lesson_line: Sell into strength. The gain you bank is the gain you keep when it falls back into the base.

wrong.Sell nothing, just trail the stop up: Sell nothing and a 5R trade can fall right back. BAC fell back into the base after 5R.
wrong.Sell a third here, at 3R: There's no fixed third at 3R. The first sell is a judgment, sold into strength.
wrong.Sell it all when it hits 5R: Selling it all gives up the trail. 5R is a place to sell some, not everything.

questions.story: Five taps of a 23.5 ceiling after a big run. You bought the breakout at 23.56 with your stop at 23.12. It's day 5 and you're up 3R.
questions.simple: Sell some into the strength, because a big run can fall right back, and the gain you bank is the gain you keep.

deeper.example: BAC, 2017-02-14: bought at 23.56 with the stop at 23.12 after five taps of the ceiling. It hit 5R in about three weeks, then fell back into the base with a low of 22.16.

reasons: B19 also says in practice he mostly waits for 5R; the hard rule is keyed

questions.q: It just triggered again. Do you buy it?
choices: Yes, as a new trade, new stop
No, one try per base
Yes, with a wider stop this time
No, wait for a new base to form
questions.answer: Yes, as a new trade, new stop
questions.why: Yes. It triggered again, so it's a new trade with every rule. New stop a few cents under Thursday's low, not wider. Size from that stop. A stop-out doesn't change the chart. If price takes the pivot back, the setup is live again. There's a limit so you don't chase a loss: 3 tries on one stock in a week, 6 in a month.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out isn't a verdict on the setup. The next trigger is a new trade.

wrong.No, one try per base: The limit is 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month, not one.
wrong.Yes, with a wider stop this time: The stop goes under the new day's low again. A wider stop to avoid a repeat is the mistake.
wrong.No, wait for a new base to form: The base is still there and it triggered again. That's the re-entry.

questions.story: You got stopped out of a flat base breakout on Tuesday. Thursday it trades back through the pivot.
questions.simple: Yes, because a stop-out doesn't kill the setup, and a new trigger is a new trade with its own stop.

deeper.trap: The trap is trading the loss. After a stop-out you want to go bigger, or give the next try more room. A new trade follows every rule again: its own stop, its own size from that stop.

questions.q: Bought at 143.20, stop 141.89. You sell a third at 147.13. How many R did that third bank?
questions.why: 3R. The gain divided by the fill minus the stop. LII broke out on light volume and still ran; the stop was tested to the cent first.
questions.lesson_line: Count every exit in R. The first third is 3R.

questions.q: On a flat base breakout, you put your stop 7% to 8% under your buy, like IBD's sell rule.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Our stop goes a few cents under the low of the day. That's where the chart says you're wrong, and on most breakouts it lands within about 3% of the buy. IBD's 7% to 8% is a general rule for how far any purchase may fall. A fixed 7% stop would lose more than twice what we take. It also ignores the chart. Stop first from the chart, then size from the stop.
questions.lesson_line: The chart picks the stop, not a percent. Then the stop picks the size.
questions.simple: False, because the low of the day shows where you're wrong, and it's closer than 7% on most breakouts.

deeper.trap: The trap is mixing two jobs. IBD's 7% to 8% caps how far a purchase may fall. Our stop comes from the chart first, and the size follows from it. A 7% stop when the low of the day is much closer is far wider than ours, and it shrinks the size.

questions.q: Textbook breakout, Red market. What do you do?
choices: Mostly cash, watch it for later
Full size, it's a textbook base
Smaller size, fewer positions
Take it, it's an A+ setup
questions.answer: Mostly cash, watch it for later
questions.why: Mostly cash. Red means the market isn't backing longs, so even a great breakout has the odds against it. The reading is a guide, not a law. But in Red I'm mostly in cash, plus shorts if you trade them. Keep this one on your list. A leader holding up while the market's Red is exactly the name to track. When the reading turns, it's one of the first you look at. Green is when we press. Yellow is smaller and fewer. Orange is A+ only.
questions.lesson_line: The best box in a Red market is still a box in a Red market. Sit on your hands.

wrong.Full size, it's a textbook base: That's Green. In Red, the chart doesn't get to override the market.
wrong.Smaller size, fewer positions: That's Yellow. Red is a step further down.
wrong.Take it, it's an A+ setup: That's Orange, A+ only. Red is mostly cash.

questions.story: Our market filter in the app reads Red today. A leader shows a textbook flat base and trades through the pivot on heavy volume.
questions.simple: Mostly cash, because in a Red market even a great chart has the odds against it, so you watch it for later.

deeper.trap: The trap is the chart pull. A textbook base on heavy volume feels like permission. The reading comes first. Green is full risk, Yellow is smaller and fewer, Orange is only A+ setups, and Red is mostly cash and shorts.

reasons: asks the ladder stance only; whether Red allows any long is an open owner question

questions.q: How many do you buy on day one?
choices: A few of the best ones
All eight, half size
Four now, four tomorrow
None, wait a week
questions.answer: A few of the best ones
questions.why: A few of the best ones. The first Green day after a correction can be a head fake. Buy all eight, it fails, and eight stops hit at once. Start with a few. If they work, the market's telling you the turn is real, and you add. If they fail, you lost a little and you're mostly in cash. Let the market earn your exposure.
questions.lesson_line: Green after a correction: a few first. Let the market earn your exposure.

wrong.All eight, half size: Eight at once is still all in. If the turn fails, eight stops hit together.
wrong.Four now, four tomorrow: That adds on the clock. You add when the first ones work, not when the calendar says.
wrong.None, wait a week: Green says you can start. Start small, don't sit out.

questions.story: The market just turned Green after a correction. You have eight flat bases sitting right at their pivots.
questions.simple: A few of the best, because a fresh Green can fail, and the first ones working is your proof to add more.

deeper.trap: Green says how much you may hold: up to 10 positions at full risk per grade. Starting with a few is how you get there after a correction. You earn the size one working position at a time.

questions.q: Write tomorrow's plan. Which one is yours?
choices: Market, stop under the low, sell a push
Market, stop at the base low, out at 2R
Limit under 90, 7% stop, third at 3R
Market, stop under the low, all out 5R
questions.answer: Market, stop under the low, sell a push
questions.why: Market order as it trades through 90, stop a few cents under that day's low, and sell some into a push. Look at today's candle first: a hammer inside yesterday's range, right under 90. That's a good look, and tomorrow is a possible buy day. Mark 90 tonight and set the alert. When it goes, you buy at market, because a limit can miss the move. The stop goes under the low of the day, where the chart says you're wrong. The first sell is a judgment, into a 3, 5 or 7 day push. Write it all down before the open, so there's no debate later.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, sell, trail. Know the plan before the trigger. Then run it without a debate.

wrong.Market, stop at the base low, out at 2R: All out at 2R gives up the trail. A base-low stop is often too far away.
wrong.Limit under 90, 7% stop, third at 3R: A limit under 90 can miss the breakout. The stop is the low of the day, not a fixed percent.
wrong.Market, stop under the low, all out 5R: The first sell is part of it, into a push. All out at once gives up the trail.

questions.story: Six weeks flat, three taps of 90, above its 50 and 200-day. It could trade through 90 tomorrow.
questions.simple: Buy at market through 90, stop under the low of the day, sell some into a push, all decided before the open.

deeper.example: NUS, 2013-09-09: it traded through 90 on 1.9x volume. Buy 90.01, stop 88.22, 2.0% under the fill. It hit 3R on day 1 and the run went to 23.5R. That's why we rarely sell on day 1.

reasons: owner rulebook E57, F62 and B19
fixed before (85.00 was not NUS's base low)

questions.q: Do you hold it through the report?
choices: No, it's not up 5R yet
Yes, the trend is still up
Only if you sell half first
Yes, the stop covers you
questions.answer: No, it's not up 5R yet
questions.why: No. We only hold through a report when the trade is up 5R. You're at 2R. A report can gap the stock right through your stop, and the stop can't catch a gap. At 5R you've got enough cushion to take that hit and still be fine. At 2R, one bad gap turns a winner into a loss. So you sell before tomorrow's close and look at it again after the report.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings is a gap you can't stop. 5R buys the ticket. 2R doesn't.

wrong.Yes, the trend is still up: The trend doesn't report earnings. The gap is the risk.
wrong.Only if you sell half first: Selling half doesn't change the test. What you hold has to be up 5R.
wrong.Yes, the stop covers you: A gap opens right through a stop. Only the 5R cushion covers you.

questions.story: Your flat base breakout is up 2R. The company reports earnings tomorrow after the close.
questions.simple: No, because a report can gap right through your stop, and only a 5R cushion pays for that risk.

deeper.trap: The trap is the trend. The base is working, so you want to stay. But earnings is a gap you can't stop. At 5R the cushion pays for it. At 2R it doesn't, whatever the chart looks like.

reasons: key rests on one rulebook fact (B22)

questions.q: Check the moving averages. Is this one we can buy?
choices: Yes, a tad extended but fine
Yes, everything lines up perfectly
No, too far over the 200-day to buy
No, wait for it to touch the 50-day
questions.answer: Yes, a tad extended but fine
questions.why: Yes, but be honest about it. It's a tad extended. About 9% over the 50-day is a stretch, and the 200-day sits way down there. So it's not a perfect picture. Here's why it's still a yes. The lines are in order: price over a rising 50, the 50 over a rising 200. And it's only about 2% over its 9 EMA. It's resting on its short-term averages, not running away. Too stretched to buy is more than 10% over the 9 EMA. Today's candle is a hammer inside yesterday's range, right under 90. That's a good look and a possible buy day. NUS broke out the next day on 1.9x volume and reached 3R the session after.
questions.lesson_line: Read the lines honestly. A tad extended can still be a buy. Under the 200-day never is.

wrong.Yes, everything lines up perfectly: The lines are in order, but it's not perfect. It's a tad extended from the 50, and the 200 is way down there.
wrong.No, too far over the 200-day to buy: Way over the 200-day is what a leader looks like. Under the 200-day is the hard no for a stock.
wrong.No, wait for it to touch the 50-day: You could wait a long time. It's resting on its short-term averages, and tomorrow can be the buy day.

questions.simple: Yes, it's a tad extended from the 50-day, but the lines are in order and it sits close to its 9 EMA.

deeper.trap: The trap is checking only the 200-day. Under it we don't buy stocks, full stop. We also want the 50 above the 200, because it shows the uptrend has been in place a while. That one is mostly a must, not always. An exception is a judgment call.

reasons: owner rulebook B26 covers the 200-day only; the 50-over-200 half is our card's rule

questions.story: The day before the breakout. It closed about 2% over its 9 EMA and about 9% over its 50-day. It's about 58% over its 200-day.

questions.q: Check the moving averages. Do they look like a leader's?
choices: No, the 50 is still under the 200
No, price is under the 200-day
Yes, price is over the 200-day
Yes, a rebound like this one leads
questions.answer: No, the 50 is still under the 200
questions.why: No. Price is over the 200-day, so it isn't off limits. But the 50-day is still under the 200, and the 200 is flat, going nowhere. It's also well stretched over its 50-day. The day it broke out, price was 14.3% over the 200-day while the 50 sat 1.6% under it. That's a stock climbing out of a downtrend, not a leader resting. I want the 50 over the 200. That's mostly a must, not always, and an exception is a judgment call. This one worked, up to 6.3R. One trade doesn't settle it either way.
questions.lesson_line: A base that works isn't always the base we look for. Check the lines first.

wrong.No, price is under the 200-day: Price is above the 200-day. The line that's off is the 50-day.
wrong.Yes, price is over the 200-day: That's one line. The 50 under the 200 says the uptrend hasn't been in place long.
wrong.Yes, a rebound like this one leads: A rebound out of a downtrend isn't a leader resting. This one worked, but that's not what we look for.

questions.simple: No, because the 50-day is still under the 200-day. It's a rebound out of a downtrend, not a leader resting.

questions.q: Left-side high 100.00. The base's first week tops out at 97.50. How far under the high is that, in percent?

questions.lesson_line: The first week stays close to the high. Measure the gap in percent.
questions.simple: The first week sits 2.5% under the high, and our card allows up to 3%, so it passes.

questions.q: Does this base pass our card's first-week test?
questions.story: The left-side high is 100.00. The base's first week, the five sessions after that high, tops out at 93.00, which is 7% under it. Then it builds a neat box between 91 and 93.
choices: No; week one fell too far below it
Yes, the box is neat
Yes, if volume dries in the box
No; a flat base needs a handle
questions.answer: No; week one fell too far below it
questions.why: No. Our card wants the base's first week to reach within 3% of the left-side high. Here the first week's highest high is 93.00, which is 7% under the top, so it fails. A neat box later does not fix week one. A flat base rests near its high from the start.
questions.lesson_line: A flat base stays near its high in week one. A quick drop fails the test, however neat the box.

wrong.Yes, the box is neat: A neat box later does not fix week one. The first week must stay near the high.
wrong.Yes, if volume dries in the box: Quiet volume is a grade cue. It cannot make up for a first week that fell away.
wrong.No; a flat base needs a handle: Handles belong to the cup. A flat base is a box and needs none.

questions.simple: No, because the first week must stay within 3% of the high, and this one fell 7%.

deeper.trap: The trap is judging the box and forgetting where it sits. The box between 91 and 93 can be perfectly tight. But week one fell 7% under the top, so the stock has not rested near its high. It has fallen away and is building a lower shelf.

reasons: the 3% first-week line is a proposed card number

questions.why: 65 weeks. 325 sessions divided by 5 sessions a week is 65 weeks. Our card allows at most 65 weeks from the left-side high to the day before the breakout. MarketSmith also puts a flat base at 5 to 65 weeks long.
questions.lesson_line: There is a ceiling on length too: 65 weeks, which is 325 sessions.
questions.simple: 325 sessions at 5 sessions a week is 65 weeks, the longest a flat base can run on our card.

1,625 weeks
81 weeks
65 weeks

questions.q: Is it a flat base breakout?
questions.story: A leader's box began at a left-side high 80 weeks ago. Price has stayed under that high since, tapping it again and again. Today it trades through it.
choices: No; it ran too long to be flat
Yes, longer is stronger
Yes, if the top is flat
No; it needs a handle first
questions.answer: No; it ran too long to be flat
questions.why: No. Our card caps a flat base at 65 weeks from the left-side high to the day before the breakout. This one went sideways for 80 weeks, so it is too long. MarketSmith puts a flat base at 5 to 65 weeks. A flat top is needed but is not enough. Past the cap it is no longer a flat base.
questions.lesson_line: A base that drags on past 65 weeks is no longer a flat base.

wrong.Yes, longer is stronger: Length has a cap. Past 65 weeks it is no longer a flat base.
wrong.Yes, if the top is flat: A flat top is needed, but not enough. The base must also be 65 weeks or less.
wrong.No; it needs a handle first: A handle belongs to the cup. The flat base fails here on length.

deeper.trap: The trap is a long, tidy base that looks strong. A flat top tapped again and again is good, but the clock matters too. At 80 weeks it is past the cap, so this is not a flat base breakout, whatever the top looks like.

questions.q: Which ceiling is the cleaner one by our card's cue?
questions.story: Two stocks rest under a flat top. Stock A made two clean taps of it, a month apart. Stock B made four, each a separate swing.
choices: Stock B, three or more taps
Stock A, fewer taps mean less supply
Both are identical on our card
Neither; a ceiling needs five taps
questions.answer: Stock B, three or more taps
questions.why: Stock B. Two or more separate touches of the top make a ceiling, so both stocks qualify. Three or more clean taps of one flat level is our card's cleaner version. It is a cue, not a gate, and the final grade stays a judgment call. Stock A still has a ceiling.
questions.lesson_line: Two taps make a ceiling. Three or more make it the cleaner one.

wrong.Stock A, fewer taps mean less supply: More clean taps of one level make the cleaner ceiling on our card, not fewer.
wrong.Both are identical on our card: Both pass as ceilings, but three or more taps is the cleaner version.
wrong.Neither; a ceiling needs five taps: Two or more separate touches make a ceiling. Five is not a rule.

questions.simple: Stock B, because three or more clean taps is the cleaner ceiling, and two taps still count.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking touches can be any days. Touches must be separate, with the first at least 10 sessions back. Four back-to-back days at the top are one push, not four taps.

reasons: card criterion is proposed; our scan found no difference for three or more taps

questions.q: Our card wants the 200-day to be no lower than it was 20 sessions ago.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. On our card the 200-day must be no lower than it was 20 sessions ago. A flat 200-day passes, and a falling one fails. This check sits beside the line order: price above the 50-day and the 200-day, with the 50 above the 200.
questions.lesson_line: Check the slope of the 200-day. It must not be falling.

questions.q: Does the context pass our card?
questions.story: A leader rests in a box above its 50-day and 200-day, with the 50-day over the 200-day. The 200-day is 41.80 today and was 42.30 twenty sessions ago.
choices: No; the 200-day is lower now
Yes, price is above both averages
Yes, the 50-day is over the 200-day
No; it needs a rising 20 EMA

questions.why: No. The 200-day is 41.80 today and was 42.30 twenty sessions ago, so it is lower. Our card wants it no lower than 20 sessions ago. Stacked averages do not make up for that. Price above both averages and the 50 over the 200 are two other checks, and all three must pass. A flat 200-day would pass.
questions.lesson_line: Stacked averages are not enough. The 200-day must not be falling.

wrong.Yes, price is above both averages: That is one check. The 200-day must also not be lower than 20 sessions ago.

questions.q: What do you do with your position?
questions.story: You're long this stock and it's working. It just ran about 20% in four days. Four green closes in a row, three of them big. It's now far above its rising 9 EMA.
choices: Sell a big piece into the run
Buy more, it's breaking out
Hold it all until the 20 EMA breaks
Sell a tiny slice, hold the rest
questions.answer: Sell a big piece into the run
questions.why: Sell a big piece into it. That's a climax run on your own long: about 20% in four days, stretched way over a rising 9 EMA. Runs like that snap back toward the average fast. The gain you're sitting on can disappear in a couple of days. So I sell a good chunk while buyers are still paying up. How big is a judgment call. Some keep going, like this one did. Plenty don't. Trail what's left on the 9 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: When a winner goes vertical, sell a big piece into it.

wrong.Buy more, it's breaking out: Whatever you call it, it's stretched way over the 9 EMA. You sell into a burst. You don't add to it.
wrong.Hold it all until the 20 EMA breaks: By the time the 20 EMA breaks, a lot of this run is gone. Sell some into the strength.
wrong.Sell a tiny slice, hold the rest: A tiny slice barely banks anything. A climax run calls for a big piece.

questions.simple: Sell a big piece, because a run that far over the 9 EMA can snap back fast. How big is your call.

deeper.example: On the chart, a climax run is price pulling far away from its 9 EMA in a few big bars. That stretch is the cue to sell into strength.
deeper.trap: Four green days in a row feel like proof. On your own long, that's the time to sell into strength, not add. Bracco's parabolic burst is the model: straight up days, gaps up, ranges getting bigger. How big a piece is a judgment call.

reasons: key rests on one rulebook fact (C34)

questions.lesson_line: Climax run: sell into strength. Do not add.
questions.simple: False, because a climax run is a time to sell a big part, not to add.

questions.q: The pivot is 48.50. The stock rips through it at the open. What's the most you'll pay before it's a chase?
questions.why: $50.44. We never buy more than 4% above the buy point, and with a market order the buy point is the pivot itself. 4% of 48.50 is 1.94. Add it to 48.50 and you get 50.44. Past that, you're chasing. Chasing costs you size. Your stop doesn't move up with your fill. So the higher you pay, the wider the stop and the fewer shares you get. Work this number out the night before.
questions.lesson_line: Know your top price before the open. Past 4%, I let it go.
questions.simple: Add 4% of the pivot to the pivot, which is 50.44, because paying more widens your stop and shrinks your size.

wrong.$46.56: You took the 4% off instead of adding it.
wrong.$48.60: That's just IBD's 10 cents over the pivot. Our line is 4%.
wrong.$1.94: That's the 4% itself. Add it to the pivot.

Nothing; taps never change the grade

questions.q: What did this stock do before it started resting?
questions.story: The day before the breakout. Check the left side of the chart.
choices: Ran up hard to new highs
Slid for months to a new low
Chopped sideways for a year
Gapped down hard on earnings
questions.answer: Ran up hard to new highs
questions.why: It ran up hard. That's the whole point of a flat base: it's a rest after a run. No run, nothing to rest from. WSM ran about 30% into this rest, then went sideways near the highs. That's what you want to see before you buy a base. Strong stocks rest. Weak ones just sit there.
questions.lesson_line: A flat base is a rest, so it needs a run first.

wrong.Slid for months to a new low: A slide ends in a bottoming pattern, not a rest near the highs.
wrong.Gapped down hard on earnings: A gap down breaks the trend. A flat base is a rest near the highs.
wrong.Chopped sideways for a year: A stock that went nowhere has nothing to rest from. A flat base follows a run.

questions.simple: It ran up hard first, because a flat base is a rest after a run. No run, nothing to rest from.
